title: Women’s hockey triumphs in home opener over UNH - The Huntington News
content: The No. 7 Northeastern women’s hockey (2-1-0, 1-0-0 Hockey East) beat the University of New Hampshire Wildcats (2-3-1, 0-1-0HE) Oct. 11, finishing with an exciting 6-3 score in the team’s first home game at Walter Brown Arena. With each goal scored by a different player, the team’s depth and young talent shined. Junior forward Éloïse Caron remained out of the lineup due to her appearance at Hockey Canada’s National Women’s Team Training Camp, and sophomore goaltender Renna Trembecky took her second stab as starting netminder. “I’ll take three points any day of the week,” associate head coach Nick Carpenito said. “I’m happy. Good game and happy to win.” The Huskies came out looking more cohesive than the game before, but lacked any shots that seriously challenged senior goaltender Noemi Martinez. Before Northeastern could find the net, UNH beat them to it. Sophomore forward Nina Rossi intercepted the puck and handed it off to senior forward Danika Botterill, who launched a shot to the lower right of the net, securing a 1-0 score 11 minutes into the opening frame. With four minutes left in the first, junior forward Morgan Jackson responded with a bar-down shot to tie the game 1-1. The goal gave the Huskies a necessary adrenaline boost, and they notched four more shots before the period finished out. Five minutes into the second period,  Northeastern went on a power play and pulled Trembecky for an extra skater in order to go six vs. four, an unusual move for the team. It was short lived, as 30 seconds later, junior forward Addison Spitz took a penalty for elbowing, putting the goaltender back in the net as Northeastern went three vs. five. Northeastern capitalized on the power play in the sixth minute of the period. The team circled the offensive zone as sophomore forward Stryker Zablocki passed to freshman forward Ivana Wey in the right faceoff circle, who found freshman forward Lilly McInerney at the backdoor. McInerney found the net, securing her and Wey’s first collegiate points. “She works so hard, she goes to the net, incredibly coachable, really smart, doesn’t feel like she plays beyond her years, like she doesn’t panic with the puck,” Carpenito said ofMcInerney. “[If] she continues to do that, she’s gonna continue to get big minutes.” To round out the power play, Jackson took the puck down the offensive zone and found senior forward Allie Lalonde at the end, whose shot was blocked. Sophomore forward Emy McDermid caught the rebound, firing it past Martinez for a 3-1 lead. In the eleventh minute, graduate student forward Grace Sadura received a penalty for cross-checking. A minute later, Zablocki went on a breakaway and was tripped by junior defender Callista Printz, landing her in the penalty box for two minutes and giving Northeastern yet another advantage for the remaining minute. The Wildcats only gained momentum in the final minutes of the period though, giving Trembecky some saves for her highlight reel. At the end of the second period, Northeastern still led in shots 27 to 13. Carpenito hopes to see more from special teams in future match-ups, he said post-game. “Special teams definitely gotta clean up, but still very early in the season, so I’m not super concerned about that right now,” he said. “It’ll come with practice and developing chemistry.” Three minutes into the third period, sophomore defender Lexi Mara took a penalty for tripping. Just three seconds later, Botterill shot from above the left faceoff circle, and Trembecky swerved at the wrong moment, putting the puck squarely in the back of the net. Two minutes later, Botterill planted at the bottom of the circle to deflect a shot from Rossi into the net, finding the 3-3 equalizer and a hat trick. In a matter of minutes, the Huskies had blown a two-goal lead and the team was rattled. Attempts to move to the offensive zone were shut down by the Wildcats, and the two played a far more back-and-forth game. It was Zablocki who bailed the team out with nine minutes remaining on the clock. Wey passed to Zablocki in the neutral zone, and she took off down the left wing before firing from the center of the circle. The puck knocked against Martinez’s knee pads in an almost save, before finding the far right of the net and putting the game at 4-3. With five minutes to go, McDermid skated down the right wing before finding Sadura by the net. Sadura fought for the puck in the crease before finding the net for a 5-3 game. Just 90 seconds later, sophomore defender Ella Lloyd skated behind the net to find sophomore forward Molly MacCurtain to the right. MacCurtain launched the puck to Martinez’s right, putting the Huskies up 6-3 with three minutes to go. Trembecky finished with 14 saves in her second start of the season, and Northeastern nearly tripled UNH’s shot count, 47 to 17, in a dominant offensive outing. “We’re sticking to the game plan or sticking to what we want to do, they’re buying in, and they’re rewarded,” Carpenito said. Northeastern will take on the No. 5 Quinnipiac University Bobcats (5-0-0, 0-0-0 ECAC) in Hamden, Conn. title: Analysts are Split on UnitedHealth Stock Before Earnings - TradingView
content: UnitedHealth Group UNH heads into its third-quarter earnings report with Wall Street divided over how much upside remains, as Piper Sandler stays bullish while TD Cowen turns more cautious on the insurer's longer-term earnings trajectory. UnitedHealth is scheduled to report Q3 results on Oct. 13. Piper Sandler analyst Jessica Tassan reiterated a Buy rating ahead of the report, while TD Cowen analyst Ryan Langston maintained a Hold rating and cut his price target to $402 from $430. Wall Street currently expects UnitedHealth to report $4.15 in EPS, up 42.1% year over year, while revenue is projected to fall about 1.6% to $111.31 billion. Piper Sandler's bullish case centers partly on Medicare Advantage. Using CMS September enrollment data, Tassan estimates that 66.8% of UnitedHealth members are enrolled in contracts rated 4 Stars or higher for 2027. She called those results resilient and underappreciated, arguing that UnitedHealth remains the most actionable Medicare Advantage name in her coverage. At roughly 14 times estimated 2028 adjusted earnings, Tassan said she would be a buyer of UNH into the quarter. Langston believes current Q3 expectations, including an 89.9% medical loss ratio, are achievable and sees possible upside from Optum Health. However, he expects management's initial 2027 outlook to be more restrained, with EPS growth guidance potentially matching or coming in below the current consensus estimate of about 14%. The latest Star Ratings also create another issue. Langston estimates the decline could result in a roughly $13 per-member-per-month revenue headwind in 2028, equivalent to about $1.5 billion in revenue impact. I think the central question for UnitedHealth investors is no longer simply whether Q3 estimates are beatable. Both analysts appear relatively comfortable with the current quarter. The bigger debate is what comes next. Piper Sandler sees an attractively valued company with resilient Medicare Advantage positioning, while TD Cowen is more concerned about 2027 growth expectations and the eventual financial impact of weaker Star Ratings. That makes management's forward commentary especially important. For investors, I would watch medical loss ratio, Optum Health profitability, initial 2027 EPS guidance and management's assessment of the 2028 Star Ratings impact. A clean quarter may help the stock, but the real catalyst could be whether UnitedHealth convinces investors that earnings growth can reaccelerate without another meaningful deterioration in Medicare economics. title: UnitedHealth shares are doing something unusual ahead of earnings - CNBC
content:
The only thing more expensive than health insurance is perhaps the costs of insuring shares of health insurers. Case in point: UnitedHealth Group, which reports earnings Tuesday. Implied volatility is running at twice realized volatility ahead of the October 13 quarterly earnings release. In other words, options prices - the cost of insuring the underlying stock - are expensive, which sets up well for short premium strategies. In the case of UnitedHealth shares, traders can sell November premium to cut the cost of a longer-dated January call by more than half. UnitedHealth heads into Tuesday’s report with much of the damage from its prior missteps already priced in. While rising healthcare costs always remain a headwind, management’s 13% to 16% EPS growth target looks achievable. The stock has basically been flat over the last five years. By the way, according to the company, 90% of United’s 52 million customers worldwide are in the U.S. By its own statistics, the company covers about 12% to 13.5% of the U.S. population. Growing enrollment is critical to EPS growth, but so too is underwriting margin. In the managed care and health insurance business, underwriting margin represents the core operational profitability generated directly from managing healthcare risk. It measures the financial return an insurer achieves strictly from collecting premiums and managing medical care. On the enrollment side, ACA marketplace-driven enrollment appears poised to decline, a headwind for revenue in a segment that had been a growth driver. Fortunately, it’s a smaller piece of the enterprise than Medicare and Commercial. Commercial fee-based enrollment grew ~2.9% YoY between 2024 and 2025, while total Medicare enrollment grew 4.5%. The commercial segment growth may not look impressive as a headline number, but given the U.S. workforce grew ~1.4% over the same period, United appears to be gaining market share. At 17 times forward earnings, and with free cash flow at 5.7% of enterprise value and 6.5% of market cap, the stock isn’t priced for any recovery. On the options side, the market is implying 40% volatility for a stock that’s been realizing 20%. Granted. The 40% number captures this week’s earnings, and it’s likely elevated because the stock has had a couple of eye-watering earnings moves in the past 8 reported quarters. In January, the stock fell almost 20% following earnings, and April 2025 saw a similar sharp decline. As it stands, UNH is about 12-13% below the midpoint of the two-year high and low. The stock has traded lower in five of the last 8 earnings. Current options prices imply a 6.5% earnings move, according to Cboe LiveVol data. That’s the second highest implied move in almost two years. Sell the November 340/420 strangle to help finance the purchase of the January 2027 400 call. Buying the Jan 400 call costs $18.20. Selling the Nov 420 call at $5.80 and the Nov 340 put at $4.80 brings in $10.60, for a net debit of about $7.60, cutting the call’s cost by roughly 58%. If UNH finishes November between 340 and 420, both short legs expire worthless and the January call is held for $7.60, with a breakeven of $407.60 at January expiration. A rally through 420 is covered by the long 400 call. The real risk is below: a close under 340 means buying shares there, for an effective basis near $347.60 including the debit. title: UNH Stock Tracks Hot Monthly Streak: Wall Street Cheers ‘Impressive’ Q2 And Sees Over 20% More Room To Run - Stocktwits
content: Shares of UnitedHealth Group, Inc. (UNH) are headed for their fourth monthly win as Wall Street turns more bullish after a large second-quarter (Q2) earnings beat and a sweeping increase to its 2026 outlook. UNH stock rose 1% on Friday, bringing its monthly gain to nearly 3%, while shares also finished the week marginally higher. BofA called UnitedHealth’s quarter “impressive,” noting that earnings beat consensus by 31% and guidance rose 12%. The firm raised its price target to $512, implying over 20% upside, while reiterating a ‘Buy’ rating and citing a “strong” quarter and broad-based outlook increase. Morgan Stanley was even more bullish, lifting its target to $529, implying a 24% upside. The firm said the Q2 beat and higher 2026 targets “validate its disciplined strategy and establish a stronger base for future growth.” Truist, Oppenheimer and KeyBanc each moved to $500 targets, implying a 17% upside. Truist highlighted top- and bottom-line beats, a better Medical Care Ratio, and improving expectations for UnitedHealthcare and Optum Health. Oppenheimer said that the company “handily” topped expectations, while KeyBanc said results “topped bullish expectations” and argued UnitedHealth could hit $30 in earnings per share (EPS) sooner than anticipated. Goldman Sachs and UBS both raised their targets to $490, implying a 15% upside. Goldman cited a “material” earnings beat, stronger Optum Health profitability and a larger-than-expected guidance increase. UBS said UnitedHealth was “making good progress with more to go.” Meanwhile, RBC Capital raised its target to $478, implying a 12% upside. It remained positive on the earnings beat and guidance hike but flagged investor concern around persistent commercial medical-cost pressure. UnitedHealth posted adjusted EPS of $6.38, beating the $4.92 consensus and rising from $4.08 a year ago. Revenue of $112.03 billion also topped estimates, while the medical care ratio improved to 86.7% from 89.4%. Additionally, the company raised its 2026 adjusted EPS outlook to $19.50-$20 from more than $18.25, lifted UnitedHealthcare’s operating profit forecast to at least $12 billion, and increased Optum Health’s outlook to at least $2.2 billion. CEO Stephen Hemsley said UnitedHealth was “returning to form” as stronger performance disciplines took hold. He reaffirmed the company’s 13%-16% long-term earnings-growth target and doubled the 2026 buyback goal to at least $5 billion. Medicare Advantage drove the beat, with costs coming in below expectations. “Medicare delivered a strong second quarter,” UnitedHealthcare CEO Tim Noel said. Commercial plans remained the weak spot, with medical-cost trends above 11%. On the other hand, Optum said its tools added nearly 200,000 patient-facing hours, cut clinician cognitive burnout by 90%, and achieved a 96% first-pass approval rate for digital prior authorizations. On Stocktwits, retail sentiment was ‘extremely bullish’ amid ‘extremely high’ message volume. One user said, “$UNH the dark horse that everyone is not seeing is their integration of AI across all business functions which will MASSIVELY cut down their overhead.” Another user said, “$UNH In Hemsley we trust!!! But yea, I think 470 - 550 might be a good exit point just looking at the historical data. Honestly, I want to hold this for a year for tax efficiency but I don't want the same CMS nightmare again in 2027/1 or at least as long as trump is in power.” For updates and corrections, email newsroom[at]stocktwits[dot]com. SpaceX (SPCX) shares rose 1% overnight heading into Monday after CEO Elon Musk dismissed a report claiming that the rocket and satellite company had placed a $52 billion order with Foxconn for Nvidia-powered AI servers. SPCX stock fell 5% on Friday, extending its weekly decline to 15%. “This is fake news,” Musk said on X in response to a post summarizing the reported agreement. Taiwan’s Economic Daily said that Hon Hai Precision Industry, better known as Foxconn, had secured its first contract to manufacture AI servers for SpaceX. According to the report, SpaceX was preparing to deploy more than 13,000 server racks built around Nvidia’s GB300 platform. The estimated $52 billion value was based on an assumed cost of $4 million per rack rather than a disclosed contract price. Citrini analyst Jukan said on X that Foxconn had displaced the dominance of Dell Technologies and Super Micro Computer in supplying AI server infrastructure to SpaceX. It also claimed deliveries would begin in late 2026 and continue into the first quarter of 2027. Chairman Young Liu has previously said Foxconn expects to capture more than 40% of the global AI server market, while shipments of advanced AI racks are projected to increase through the end of the year. A separate Wall Street Journal report on Friday said that SpaceX was in discussions with the U.S. Department of Defense about supplying data-center capacity worth several billion dollars for military AI workloads. The talks were said to be ongoing and could still fail to produce an agreement. SpaceX has also explored offering computing power to outside AI customers as it seeks to compete more directly with cloud infrastructure providers such as CoreWeave. In June, SpaceX also reached computing arrangements with Google and Anthropic. The Google deal covered access to about 110,000 Nvidia chips, while Anthropic secured capacity at the company’s Colossus 1 data center in Memphis. The potential Defense Department arrangement would deepen SpaceX’s already extensive relationship with the U.S. military. The Pentagon relies on the company for rocket launches, satellite communications and missile-tracking systems. It is also seeking more computing capacity as intelligence agencies and military units increase their use of AI. SpaceX employees have reportedly discussed selling computing capacity at prices designed to compete with established cloud and specialized AI infrastructure providers. The Pentagon, meanwhile, is seeking funding for a new AI Arsenal initiative centered on access to high-end chips and computing resources. The military has also approved multiple tech companies, including SpaceX, Amazon, Google, Microsoft and Oracle, for classified AI-related work. South Korea’s Kospi as well as Samsung stock fell 4.3% each, while SK Hynix shares were down 4% in local afternoon time. The two stocks together account for roughly 60% of the Kospi’s market capitalization, making it one of the most concentrated major equity indices in the world. SK Hynix's U.S. listed stock declined 0.3% in the overnight session. As of the last close, they have declined by about 10% from the opening price on the first day of trading on Jul. 10. The Direxion Daily South Korea Bull 3X Shares (KORU), a three-times leveraged ETF tracking South Korea’s largest stocks, was down 2%. U.S. memory stocks Micron and SanDisk were holding in the green, rebounding after a dismal weekly performance. Citigroup on Monday downgraded the South Korean market to “neutral,” ending an overweight stance held since mid-2025 due to heightened market volatility, according to a report in South China Morning Post. The move was driven by extreme volatility in chip stocks and a reduced exposure to AI-themed trades. The firm added that it remains long-term bullish on AI, but has turned more cautious on Korea in the near term. Since the start of July, investors have been rotating out of semiconductor and AI infrastructure names and back into large-cap technology and software stocks, marking a shift after months of chip-led gains. Memory makers such as Micron, Samsung and SK Hynix, along with other AI hardware suppliers, have come under pressure as investors question whether the explosive AI infrastructure spending can continue at the same pace. Meanwhile, money has flowed into software and Big Tech names – including Apple, Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon and Meta – as investors seek companies that are better positioned to monetize AI through applications and services rather than infrastructure alone. The rotation also reflects profit-taking in richly valued chip stocks ahead of earnings season. Alphabet will be the first of the tech majors to report this season, with its announcement scheduled for Wednesday, followed by Intel the next day. GOOGL has gained 11% year to date, while INTC rallied 156%, underscoring how investors piled into chip stocks in 2026. ARK Investment Management founder-CEO Cathie Wood cheered Eli Lilly’s $3.8 billion AtaiBeckley acquisition on Sunday, calling it a “well-deserved” payoff for shareholders and a validation of Christian Angermayer’s psychedelic vision. ATAI stock rose 1% on Friday, adding 40% over the past five sessions and marking its best week in more than a year. Shares, however, were dipping more than 1% in overnight trading heading into Monday. Wood highlighted on X the biotech company’s role in bringing psychedelic medicines closer to mainstream clinical use: “Not only a well-deserved return for ATAI shareholders, this transaction validates Christian’s heartfelt mission and vision,” Wood said. She called Angermayer’s work with ATAI “one of the biggest catalysts of the psychedelic renaissance,” adding that clinical trials are increasingly validating the potential of psychedelics in treatment-resistant depression, post-traumatic stress disorder and broader mental health conditions. Wood also credited Angermayer with backing the field long before psychedelic medicine became widely accepted, fashionable, or investable. “Long before psychedelics were accepted, fashionable, or investable, Christian’s life’s mission was to reactivate them and bring back hope and health for those who had lost both,” she said. Wood’s praise came after ARK Invest reduced its ATAI stake last week. The ARK Genomic Revolution ETF (ARKG) sold 1.12 million ATAI shares worth about $6.02 million. As of Friday, however, ARKG still held 3.19 million shares valued at $22.78 million, or 1.4% of the fund. Lilly was also ARKG’s seventh-largest holding, with 61,258 shares worth $71.62 million and a 4.4% weighting. Eli Lilly said last week that it would acquire AtaiBeckley for up to $3.8 billion for the psychedelic drug developer as it builds out its neuroscience pipeline. Under the deal, shareholders would receive $6.75 in cash per ATAI share, with Lilly committing $2.8 billion at closing and an additional $1 billion for future milestones. The deal marked a 26% premium to AtaiBeckley’s shareholders. The companies are targeting completion of the acquisition in the third quarter of 2026. The centerpiece of the deal is BPL-003, an intranasal psychedelic therapy being tested in late-stage studies for treatment-resistant depression. Jefferies has projected that the drug could eventually generate $1 billion to $2 billion in sales if the program succeeds. AtaiBeckley has said the first late-stage data are expected in early 2029. Angermayer reflected on the deal over the weekend in an X post, saying ATAI’s next phase is about commercialization rather than advocacy. “Ten years ago, psychedelics needed an evangelist. Today, they need commercialization,” he said. After first exploring psychedelics in 2014, Angermayer helped launch Compass Pathways and ATAI in 2017 and invested more than $100 million of his own capital in ATAI. The two companies later raised over $1.5 billion, went public and helped build clinical credibility for psychedelic medicine. title: UNH Research Finds Disparities in How Communities Are Identified for Support - University of New Hampshire
content: Whether a community is prioritized for public support can depend on how its needs are measured, according to new UNH research. The study found significant differences in how government screening tools identify communities, particularly in rural areas where those differences could affect access to funding. Researchers compared four environmental justice screening tools, which use data on factors such as income, pollution, and health to identify communities that may need additional public support. Three were developed by the White House, the Department of Energy (DOE), and the Department of Transportation (DOT), while the fourth was developed by New York state. Nationally, the DOE tool designated about 18% of census tracts as disadvantaged, compared with about 35% for the White House and DOT tools. In New York state, more than half of census tracts (51.3%) were identified as disadvantaged by at least one of the four tools, but only about 14% were identified that way by all four. "We expected some differences, since each agency has its own mission. What surprised us was how large they were and how often they came from choices that aren't obvious from the documentation," says Qingran Li, assistant professor of economics at UNH's Peter T. Paul College of Business and Economics. "The tools also disagreed more for rural communities, where resources tend to be more constrained, and investment may have historically lagged." The study, published in Nature Communications, was conducted by Li; Stephen Bird, director of UNH's Carsey School of Public Policy; Susan Powers of Clarkson University; and Thomas Robbins of Schneider Electric. Urban areas were more consistently identified as disadvantaged across the four tools. The DOE tool did not designate any rural New York census tracts as disadvantaged, while New York’s own tool identified the greatest number of rural and suburban communities. The researchers note there is no single formula for measuring disadvantage. Screening tools can consider factors such as income, health, transportation access, environmental conditions and climate risks, but they don't necessarily use the same factors or assign them the same weight. They also differ in whether a community is compared with others nationwide, within its state or within its region. New York's tool, for example, accounts for regional differences, making it more likely that less urbanized communities are identified as disadvantaged. "One of the things we saw in some of the federal tools is that rural areas often are not highly prioritized, in part because environmental problems are diffuse, but the economic vulnerabilities in those areas are very real," Bird says. The findings also offer lessons for states like New Hampshire, where rural communities face challenges similar to those in New York's North Country, Bird notes. "Many rural burdens look different from urban ones, such as long distances with limited transportation options, an aging population, high heating costs, and reliance on fuel oil or propane. Tools built mainly around urban pollution, or around income measured against national or statewide benchmarks, may not fully capture those conditions," Li says. "For example, a rural New Hampshire town with moderate incomes but very high energy costs and long drives to healthcare services could be designated disadvantaged by one tool and not by another. That could affect its eligibility for weatherization, clean energy, or transportation funding." While the federal government is no longer using the three screening tools examined in the study, many states and nonprofit organizations continue to use similar tools to identify vulnerable communities, direct funding, and inform policy decisions. New York, for instance, requires at least 35% of the benefits from its clean-energy investments to go to communities designated as disadvantaged under the state's tool. Despite the differences identified in the study, Bird says the screening tools represented an important advance in public policy. "These tools were the first attempts to quantify what disadvantage means in a way that can be constructively used for public policy," Bird says. "That was a massive leap from vague discussions of 'rural areas' or 'environmental justice.'" The researchers aren't arguing against the development of screening tools or suggesting that every agency should use the same one. Instead, they say policymakers should clearly define what they want a tool to accomplish and understand how its design shapes which communities it identifies. "My biggest hope is that they can more clearly outline the focus or goals in the tool outcomes, and link the design of the tools to those goals," Bird says. "That was the thing that was pretty fuzzy in all this." Li adds, "Every screening tool embeds priorities: which burdens count, how much each one counts, and whether communities are compared nationally, statewide, or regionally. Those priorities should match the goals of the program using the tool." Copyright © 2026 , University of New Hampshire. All rights reserved.

title: Heartbreak in Orono: Maine field hockey falls to UNH in overtime - The Maine Campus
content: ORONO, Maine — The University of Maine field hockey team watched a two-goal lead disappear Friday, Oct. 9, as the University of New Hampshire stormed back to force overtime before scoring the game-winner with just over a minute remaining. This resulted in a heartbreaking 4-3 loss for Maine. Maine entered the contest ranked No. 43 in Division I, with a 5-5 overall record and a 1-0 conference record. The Black Bears were fresh off a 1-0 road loss to Towson University and a 3-1 home victory over the University at Albany. “We went into that game knowing that they were a really strong team, but knowing that we’d been working super hard that week,” second-year forward Martha Barratt said before Friday’s game. “To come away with such a convincing win, I think it has boosted our confidence a lot going into the next few weeks.” Head coach Josette Babineau also praised the team’s performance against UAlbany, highlighting the energy and effort that Maine would need to carry into its matchup with New Hampshire. “We had a very quick start in the game and just kept the energy going throughout,” Babineau said. “The effort was pretty consistent from beginning to end.” On the other side, UNH was only 2-6 but played a remarkably difficult schedule, which helped the Wildcats earn a No. 36 ranking in the Ratings Percentage Index (RPI), making them the highest-ranked America East school. New Hampshire was coming off a 1-0 conference-opening win against the University of Vermont and a 5-0 loss against Miami University in Ohio. Friday’s contest was an end-to-end affair, with a tightly contested first quarter featuring a late Maine goal that put the Black Bears up 1-0. The goal was scored by Barratt. She helped Maine make it 2-0, picking up an assist as fourth-year defender Eloise Penty slotted the ball home in the second quarter. Following halftime, New Hampshire came out looking reinvigorated and opened the scoring in the second half less than four minutes in, as first-year midfielder Delilah Talbot blasted a shot into the net. Maine responded quickly and extended its lead back to two when Barratt scored her second goal of the day. UNH would not let Maine leave the quarter with that two-goal lead, though. A few minutes later, first-year midfielder Sophie Godwin beat Maine’s defense to cut the deficit to one, putting the score at 3-2 in Maine’s favor heading into the final quarter. The final quarter was a back-and-forth affair, and UNH tied the game at 3-3 early in the quarter as Godwin found the net, scoring unassisted for the second time. From there, both teams’ defenses held strong, and the game went to overtime. The defensive battle continued, with neither team able to find the winning goal. With just over a minute remaining, first-year forward Julianna Casucci scored the game-winning goal, allowing New Hampshire to steal a crucial conference and rivalry win on the road. New Hampshire dominated the shot battle, taking 18 shots in total, with 15 on target, compared to Maine’s four shots, three of which were on goal. All three of Maine’s shots on goal resulted in scores against Wildcat third-year goalie Kerigan Ross, while first-year goalkeeper Annabel Halkes made 11 saves for the Black Bears. The loss drops Maine to 5-6 overall and 1-1 in America East play. The Black Bears will look to bounce back Sunday against No. 78 Merrimack (1-9) before traveling to face No. 49 Bryant (6-5) on Friday. After surrendering a two-goal lead against New Hampshire, Maine will need to regroup quickly as it looks to get back on track in conference play.

Arbutus Biopharma (ABUS) stock rose 6% on Thursday after the company announced new international patent lawsuits, receipt of a large settlement payment from Moderna and plans to return up to $230 million to shareholders. The stock is now on track for its best day since May 2026 after five consecutive days of trading in the red. On July 8, Arbutus received around $178 million from Moderna, the company said. This represents its share of the payment under the March 2026 global settlement that resolved all patent litigation over Moderna’s COVID-19 vaccines. In March, Arbutus and its partner Genevant Sciences, a unit of Roivant Sciences (ROIV), reached a global settlement with Moderna worth up to $2.25 billion to resolve a long-running dispute over technology used in Moderna’s COVID-19 vaccines. Under the agreement, Moderna is required to make a $950 million upfront payment to both parties, and the payout on July 8 was part of it. The remaining will be paid to Genevant under the settlement agreement. The Moderna patent litigation centered on whether Moderna had used Arbutus’s patented technology without permission in its COVID-19 vaccine. At its core, the dispute was over lipid nanoparticles (LNPs), the tiny fat particles that protect and deliver mRNA into human cells. Without effective LNPs, mRNA vaccines like Moderna’s covid vaccine Spikevax would not work well. Arbutus had developed and patented specific LNP formulations years before the pandemic. Arbutus now expects a dividend from Roivant in the third quarter, owing to its stake in the Genevant parent. Arbutus said it expects to begin returning up to about $230 million to shareholders through share repurchases starting in the third quarter. The buybacks may take the form of a tender offer, open-market purchases, or other methods and will follow receipt of the expected Genevant dividend. However, there is no assurance of the share repurchase activity, the company noted. Following the successful payout from Moderna, Arbutus and Genevant also filed three lawsuits against Pfizer Inc., BioNTech SE and certain of their affiliates to enforce patents covering lipid nanoparticle (LNP) technology used in their mRNA COVID-19 vaccines. Cases were lodged in Canada’s Federal Court and two proceedings at the Unified Patent Court in Europe. The company seeks damages and injunctions against Pfizer/BioNTech’s vaccines and any future infringing products. These actions expand an ongoing U.S. patent case in New Jersey. For years, the race to build better artificial intelligence centered on making models bigger, feeding them more data, and expanding the amount of information they could process at once. Now, a fresh frontier is emerging as researchers increasingly explore smarter memory management as another way to build more capable AI systems. Two academic papers published this month, AutoMem and SelfMem, argue that memory shouldn't be a rigid feature engineered by developers using static rules. Instead, they propose that AI systems can learn to manage their own memories. They take different approaches: AutoMem trains AI to manage an external memory system, while SelfMem lets agents refine their own memory strategies through feedback, and both report substantial gains on long-horizon benchmarks. Imagine working with an AI coding assistant on a project for months. Instead of repeatedly reminding it about your project's architecture and coding style, a smarter memory system could retain the decisions that matter while discarding obsolete information. Researchers believe that this kind of selective memory will become increasingly important as AI agents take on longer-running tasks. One way developers have tried to build more capable chatbots is by expanding their context windows, which are the immediate digital scratchpad an AI considers during a conversation. While larger context windows let models process more information, they also increase computational costs and don't necessarily help AI distinguish useful information from irrelevant details. The papers instead explore an alternative approach based on active memory curation. In AutoMem, Stanford University researchers introduced a memory manager that decides when to create, update, search, and delete records, allowing the AI to maintain a compact memory instead of continuously accumulating information. Tested on grueling, complex video games like NetHack and Crafter, this memory-management approach slashed the agent's memory growth rate by 95% and doubled its task performance, allowing a 32-billion-parameter open-weight model to perform competitively with frontier models including Claude Opus 4.5 and Gemini 3.1 Pro Thinking on the evaluated long-horizon benchmarks. SelfMem takes a completely parameter-free approach. Instead of editing model weights, it gives the AI a dedicated workspace and tools to inspect an unchangeable transcript store. It allows the agent to inspect, write, review, and revise its own memory, outperforming traditional retrieval pipelines by more than 40% on the BEAM benchmark while using only a fraction of the computational cost. The push for smarter memory comes as AI companies shift from one-off chatbots to autonomous agents designed to work over days or weeks. Whether writing software, tracking supply chains, or managing research projects, these systems must retain relevant information while discarding details that no longer matter. That is where autonomous memory management changes the equation. Instead of forcing a user to repeatedly copy-paste instructions, an agent equipped with an optimized memory workflow seamlessly recalls structural boundaries, tracks cumulative progress, and discards transient data that is no longer relevant. Better memory could also reduce the computational cost of repeatedly processing the same information, a potential advantage as AI companies look to deploy agents more efficiently at scale. Over the past year, leading AI companies like OpenAI, Google, and Anthropic have introduced basic memory features, allowing consumer chatbots to retain user preferences and custom instructions across distinct chat sessions. Today's commercial memory features generally rely on predefined mechanisms for deciding what information is retained. AutoMem and SelfMem instead point toward AI systems capable of independently evaluating and regulating their own memories. As tech companies race to build AI systems capable of executing truly long-horizon work, the findings suggest memory management may become an increasingly important complement to larger models. Future AI systems may be judged not only by how much they know, but also by how effectively they decide what information is worth keeping. Lucid Motors (LCID) shares rose for a second straight day on Thursday after the electric vehicle maker forcefully rejected reports that it was considering bankruptcy or a take-private transaction, rebounding from a brutal selloff earlier in the week. The stock traded 12% higher at the time of writing and is on track to clock its best week since July 2025, thanks to a 29% jump on Wednesday, if gains hold. The stock’s dramatic rise and fall started after an Electric-Vehicles.com report on Tuesday said that restructuring adviser AlixPartners has outlined scenarios to the company’s board, including taking the company private or seeking Chapter 11 protection. The stock fell as much as 50% on the news, but pared gains after the company refuted the report as “completely false.” “The company has sufficient liquidity to carry its operations well into next year, as recently published in its last quarterly filings, and it has not formed any special Board committee to explore the scenarios reported today,” Lucid said in a statement to Stocktwits. They further didn't suggest either option to the company management or board, it added. The company also delivered a cease and desist letter to the publication stating that the company “unequivocally denies the central factual assertions” in the article. Lucid’s new CEO, Silvio Napoli, also said in a post on LinkedIn that the claims circulated were “far from the facts” and that he looks forward to providing a full update on its quarterly earnings call on August 4. Lucid, majority-owned by Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund (PIF), has faced significant headwinds as an electric vehicle maker. Napoli replaced CFO Taoufiq Boussaid with automotive finance veteran Alexander De Bock, appointed new executives for technology, customer, digital, and transformation roles, flattened the reporting structure by halving direct reports to the CEO, and eliminated the COO position. These moves followed June layoffs of roughly 1,500 employees, about 18% of the workforce, and the removal of a second production shift at the Arizona plant, aimed at delivering roughly $158 million in annual savings. Financially, Lucid continues to face steep losses and negative gross margins despite revenue growth. In the first quarter, it posted revenue of $282.5 million, up 20% year-over-year, but recorded a net loss of approximately $1.03 billion. The company has relied heavily on its majority shareholder, Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund, for support. title: College football: UNH drops overtime heartbreaker to North Carolina A&T - AOL.com
content: GREENSBORO, N.C. — Logan Perez caught eight passes for 136 yards and two touchdowns, but the University of New Hampshire football team fell to North Carolina A&T, 30-27, in overtime Saturday at Truist Stadium. Perez recorded career highs in receptions and receiving yards while hauling in touchdown passes of 75 and 21 yards for the first scores of his collegiate career. Brooks Bentley completed 23 of 35 passes for 267 yards and two touchdowns, both to Perez. Joquez Smith rushed 20 times for a game-high 76 yards and added three receptions for 18 yards. Defensively, Trevor Barry led UNH with 10 tackles, while Sean Webb added seven stops. Josh Fillion and Ryan Blagg each blocked a punt in the first half. North Carolina A&T's Asher Holland kicked a 34-yard field goal in overtime after the Wildcats came up empty on their opening possession of the extra period. The Aggies were paced by quarterback Kevin White, who threw for 230 yards and three touchdowns while rushing for 38 yards. Michael Carlock-Williams totaled 129 receiving yards, including a 32-yard touchdown reception, and Terry Radford finished with 17 tackles. UNH dropped to 2-5 overall and 1-3 in the CAA, while North Carolina A&T improved to 2-5 overall and 2-2 in conference play.
